title: M$^2$-Miner: Multi-Agent Enhanced MCTS for Mobile GUI Agent Data Mining
one_liner: Automatically mine high-quality mobile app trajectories by letting several agents search, coordinate, and judge candidate interaction paths inside a Monte Carlo tree search loop.
lead: A mobile GUI agent learns from trajectories that pair an intent with a successful sequence of taps, swipes, and text entries. Building that data by hand is expensive, and earlier automatic miners often produce shallow or failed trajectories because they do not search carefully enough or filter quality well enough. This paper proposes M2-Miner, which combines Monte Carlo tree search with a three-agent workflow. InferAgent proposes what the user may want to do and what action could move the app toward that goal. OrchestraAgent manages search progress and coordinates which branches should be expanded next. JudgeAgent evaluates candidate trajectories so the final dataset keeps successful, diverse, and instruction-following behavior.

problem.h2: Why GUI data mining is harder than it looks
paras: A useful mobile assistant needs examples of how to complete many tasks across many app screens. Each example must include an intent, the sequence of interface states, and the actions that actually complete the task. Manual annotation can produce clean data, but it scales poorly because a person must interact with many screens and verify each trajectory.

Automatic mining has its own failure modes. Random exploration wastes time on dead ends, and a single planning agent may repeat narrow patterns or miss rare intents. GUI environments are especially difficult because every action changes the visible interface, so a small mistake early can push the search into an irrelevant part of the app.

callout.html: Use tree search to explore candidate interaction paths, and use specialized agents to propose, coordinate, and judge those paths because data quality depends on both search coverage and search discipline.

steps.text: Read the visible mobile interface and list the actions that can be taken from the current screen.
Use Monte Carlo tree search to choose which state-action branch to explore next, because the miner must balance promising paths and less-visited paths.
InferAgent suggests intents and actions, OrchestraAgent organizes search progression, and JudgeAgent checks whether a trajectory is valid and worth keeping.
Extract additional useful intents from completed trajectories, because one path can satisfy several distinct user requests.

Periodically improve the mining model with newly collected data so later search succeeds more often and reaches harder tasks, because the search policy then starts from better estimates of which actions tend to work.

paras: The paper changes how intent-trajectory data is collected. Instead of depending on manual annotation or one-shot automatic exploration, it builds the dataset through guided search with explicit quality control at each stage.
object.object: the mined dataset of mobile intents paired with successful trajectories

hidden.name: expected usefulness of an unexplored branch
paras: The hidden quantity is how likely a partially explored branch is to produce a high-quality training example if more search budget is spent on it. That quantity is not directly visible from the current screen because a branch can look unpromising now and still lead to a valuable task completion two or three actions later.

Monte Carlo tree search is useful here because it keeps statistics about which branches have succeeded before and which branches have not been explored enough. The agents then refine that estimate. InferAgent supplies semantic guesses about what the user may intend, OrchestraAgent keeps the search organized, and JudgeAgent adjusts the quality estimate by rejecting weak trajectories.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark branches that are more likely to repay more search with reusable supervision.

reads.html: The search must keep asking which unfinished path is most worth one more step.

The method estimates branch value from search outcomes, agent proposals, and quality judgments, because the miner must allocate limited exploration budget toward branches that can yield valid and diverse trajectories.

mechanism.h2: Why the search-and-judge loop improves the data
paras: Monte Carlo tree search helps because GUI mining is a sequential decision problem with branching choices. The search tree stores which actions have already been tried from each interface state and how often those choices eventually led to success. That memory prevents the miner from repeating the same poor branch blindly and gives it a way to revisit underexplored branches when they still look promising.

The multi-agent design matters because search quality depends on more than one skill. InferAgent contributes semantic guesses about plausible user intents and next actions, which makes expansion steps more targeted. OrchestraAgent keeps the full process coherent by deciding how the agents' outputs affect the tree search. JudgeAgent filters candidate trajectories, which matters because a large dataset is only useful when the recorded action sequence actually matches the intent and reaches a sensible end state.

Intent recycling increases data richness because one successful interaction path often supports several legitimate instructions. A sequence that opens an order page, updates an address, and confirms the change can serve multiple user intents depending on how the request is phrased. Reusing that path from several intent views increases instruction diversity without requiring a new expensive search run.

stages.s: current mobile app state and possible actions
tree search selects a branch to expand
specialized agents propose intent, control expansion, and judge quality
successful paths generate more intents and update the mining model
a larger and cleaner intent-trajectory dataset

math.words: A tree-search miner can choose a branch by combining two pieces: how often the branch has produced good trajectories already, and how underexplored the branch still is. Agent judgments can be folded into the branch reward so that branches producing valid data are favored.
symbols: one partial trajectory in the search tree
the current estimate of how useful this branch is for producing valid training data
extra value for branches that have not been tried enough
the score used to decide which branch to expand next

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose branch A has produced good trajectories often, so its quality estimate is 7.
Suppose branch B has produced good trajectories only once, so its quality estimate is 4, but it has been explored very little, so its exploration bonus is 4.
Branch A gets score 7 plus 1, for 8.
Branch B gets score 4 plus 4, for 8.
The miner can now revisit branch B because it may still hide valuable data that branch A has already revealed.

math.note: The paper uses a full search procedure with agent guidance, but this score captures the main idea: reward branches that look useful and branches that remain uncertain.

items.b: The judge can enforce the wrong standard.
items.html: If JudgeAgent accepts trajectories that merely reach some terminal screen without matching the intent, then the miner will collect misleading supervision and later training will copy that mismatch.

items.b: Search can still miss rare but useful paths.
items.html: Tree search allocates budget where it expects value. If a rare task requires several low-reward setup steps before payoff appears, the miner may abandon that branch early.

A successful path may support multiple interpretations, but not every alternate phrasing is equally precise. If recycled intents are too broad, the same action sequence may be paired with instructions that do not really mean the same thing.
The framework works best when search statistics, semantic proposals, and quality judgment are calibrated to the same goal: keep only trajectories that are both successful and instruction-faithful.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Set up a small Android emulator benchmark with several apps and a finite list of user tasks. Compare three miners: random exploration, single-agent guided exploration, and M2-Miner. Keep the same action budget for each method and log the resulting intent-trajectory pairs.

The demo should show that M2-Miner collects more successful and more diverse examples because it spends search budget on promising branches and filters weak trajectories before they enter the dataset. Then fine-tune the same GUI agent on each dataset and compare downstream task success.
demo.metric_eq: data_yield = valid_intent_trajectory_pairs divided by search_steps ; downstream_gain = task_success_trained_on_M2_Miner minus task_success_trained_on_baseline_data
demo.closing: The key proof is not only that the miner finds more paths. It must show that the extra paths are useful enough to train a better GUI agent afterward, because downstream task success is the only reason to collect more trajectories in the first place.
